Rebound

/rih-BOWND/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Rebound means to bounce back quickly after a decline, setback, or failure

Rebound means to bounce back quickly after a decline, setback, or failure. After falling sharply in the spring, the technology stocks began to rebound as investor confidence returned.

Worked Example

After tearing a ligament in June, the sprinter worked through months of physical therapy and managed to rebound in time for the national championships.

The sprinter suffered a real setback, the injury, and then recovered quickly enough to compete again. That fast recovery after a decline is exactly what it means to rebound.

How Rebound Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

recover

recover: to return to a normal state after trouble

rally

rally: to regain strength after a dip

revive

revive: to come back to life or vigor

Antonyms

slump

slump: to fall suddenly and heavily

collapse

collapse: to fail suddenly and completely

How Strong Is It? — stabilize → rebound → surge

stabilize vs. rebound

stabilize vs. rebound: To stabilize is only to stop falling, while to rebound is to climb back up after the fall.

surge vs. rebound

surge vs. rebound: To rebound is to return to earlier strength, but to surge is to shoot far past it.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: back

Root — bound

Root — bound: to leap (from French bondir)

Put it together

Put it together: Re- means back and bound means to leap, so rebound literally means to leap back, the way a ball springs back up off the floor or sales spring back after a slump.

Use the root in a new word: bound

Use the root in a new word: bound: With one powerful bound, the kangaroo cleared the dry creek bed.

Word Choice

Neutral / everyday

Common in news and sports writing, especially in collocations like 'rebound from a loss' and 'the market rebounded.' Do not confuse this verb with the basketball noun sense, where a rebound names the ball bouncing off the rim.
